Injection 3 already reached the maximum CRF; shorten its gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates slope sensitivity, especially for the marginal R = 1.65 pair.

Shorten the successful gradient by another grid step to seek faster separation while retaining the maximum CRF. The minimum resolution of 2.09 provides headroom, with the early pair now likely to become limiting as the gradient steepens.
Shorten the gradient one more step while holding solvent endpoints and temperature fixed. This tests whether the early pair, currently at R = 1.84, remains fully resolved in a faster method.

The early pair is barely resolved at R = 1.52, so lower the starting organic fraction to test whether increased early retention restores resolution margin. Keep tG and temperature fixed before attempting further shortening.

Raise temperature one grid step to shorten retention and measure its effect on the limiting early pair. Injection 12 provides a fully resolved reference, allowing a clean test of temperature selectivity before further gradient compression.

Heating reduced early-pair resolution, so test a lower temperature to improve selectivity while shortening the gradient to four minutes. This seeks a faster maximum-CRF method, with cooling intended to offset the resolution loss from the steeper gradient.

Test the shortest allowed gradient, using further cooling to compensate for compression of the limiting early pair. Keep the solvent endpoints unchanged to seek a faster fully resolved method than injection 14.

Lower temperature one grid step while retaining the shortest gradient to improve the early pair from R = 1.41 toward full resolution. All other pairs have substantial margin, and the modest retention increase should still leave this method faster than injection 14.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward by 0.05, preserving gradient slope while increasing final elution strength to accelerate the last peak, which currently elutes during the hold. This tests whether the early pair retains full resolution in a faster method.

Shift both endpoints upward another grid step while preserving the successful gradient slope and temperature. The previous shift shortened the last retention time without sacrificing early-pair resolution, so this tests further acceleration at maximum CRF.

Shift both endpoints upward one more grid step, keeping slope and temperature unchanged. This should further shorten the last peak’s retention while testing whether the early pair maintains its current R = 1.61.

Raise only the starting organic fraction to narrow the gradient window and seek earlier final elution. The shallower slope may help resolution, but this run will test whether reduced initial retention compromises the early pair.
Raise temperature one step to shorten the fastest fully resolved method, using the early pair’s improved R = 1.77 as resolution margin. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect.

Test one higher starting organic fraction while holding the other settings at the fastest fully resolved method. This probes whether narrowing the gradient can shorten final retention further without pushing the early pair below R = 1.5.

Return to the successful starting fraction and test one temperature step above injection 21 to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The early pair may fall below R = 1.5, but this isolates the remaining temperature adjustment that could shorten the fastest fully resolved method.

Return to the successful 30 C temperature and lower the final organic fraction one step to make the gradient shallower and increase early-pair resolution margin. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF alternative to injection 21, accepting a modest increase in final retention.

Lower injection 24’s temperature one step to improve the limiting early-pair resolution while retaining the shortest programmed gradient. The maximum CRF is already secured; this final run seeks additional resolution margin with only a small expected retention-time increase.
